meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My way of joking is to tell the truth. That's the funniest joke in the world'?
meta.ogDescription: It's George Bernard Shaw, not Muhammad Ali — spoken by Peter Keegan in John Bull's Other Island, Act II (1904, published 1907).

answer.label: Not Muhammad Ali — actually George Bernard Shaw
answer.sourceLine: The line belongs to Peter Keegan, the defrocked priest in Shaw’s comedy John Bull’s Other Island, Act II — written and staged in 1904, published 1907. Shaw’s wording is “It’s the funniest joke in the world”; the version pinned on Muhammad Ali swaps in “That’s.”

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Act II — spoken by Peter Keegan to Nora Reilly

source.excerpt:
NORA. But really and truly now, weren’t the people rather disappointing? I should think the girls must have seemed rather coarse and dowdy after the foreign princesses and people? But I suppose a priest wouldn’t notice that.

KEEGAN. It’s a priest’s business to notice everything. I won’t tell you all I noticed about women; but I’ll tell you this. The more a man knows, and the farther he travels, the more likely he is to marry a country girl afterwards.

NORA. You’re joking, Mr Keegan: I’m sure yar.

KEEGAN. My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
trail: The exact line is spoken by Peter Keegan in Act II of Shaw’s play, confirmed word-for-word in the Project Gutenberg full text of John Bull’s Other Island ↗.
Wikiquote lists it among Shaw’s sourced quotations ↗, cited to John Bull’s Other Island (1907), Act II.
Quote Investigator ↗ quotes the Keegan line while tracing related sayings, and notes the play was written in 1904 and published in 1907.
Wikipedia ↗ confirms Shaw wrote the play in 1904 and that it premiered at the Royal Court Theatre on 1 November 1904.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish dramatist and critic whose plays — Man and Superman, Pygmalion, Saint Joan — made comedy a vehicle for argument. He specialised in characters who disarm opponents by saying exactly what they mean, which is precisely the joke Peter Keegan makes in John Bull’s Other Island. Shaw won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.

misattribution.heading: The Muhammad Ali problem
misattribution.intro: Ali is credited with this line across essentially every large quote database, always in a slightly altered form and never with a source attached.

items.why: A-Z Quotes carries the wording “That’s the funniest joke in the world” under Ali’s name and dates the entry to a Twitter post of 30 July 2009 ↗, with no book, interview or broadcast behind it.

Shaw’s text reads “It’s the funniest joke in the world” — confirmed in the Project Gutenberg full text ↗. The Ali-branded version substitutes “That’s,” the usual signature of a line passed along by memory rather than copied from a page.
Wikiquote files the line in its sourced Shaw section ↗ under John Bull’s Other Island (1907), Act II.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Shaw’s, written for a fictional Irish priest in 1904 — nearly four decades before Muhammad Ali was born (1942) — and are there in the play’s Act II text ↗ to be read.

context.heading: Why Keegan says it
lead: Peter Keegan is Shaw’s holy fool — a priest stripped of his parish who wanders the Irish countryside seeing more clearly than anyone with a job. In Act II he tells Nora Reilly that the more a man knows and the farther he travels, the likelier he is to end up marrying a country girl. She assumes he is teasing her.

His reply is the play’s thesis in one sentence: the truth, said plainly in a world organised around polite evasion, lands as comedy. It is also a fair description of Shaw’s own method across four decades of playwriting.
context.detailsSummary: How the line drifted to Muhammad Ali
detailsBody: Ali is one of the internet’s strongest quote magnets: he was genuinely funny, genuinely blunt, and genuinely quotable, so aphorisms about truth-telling and bravado attach to him easily. A Shaw line about joking by telling the truth reads as something Ali could have said in a press conference — which is exactly the condition under which misattribution spreads.
The quote-database trail is thin. A-Z Quotes dates its Ali entry to a Twitter post of 30 July 2009 and offers no book, interview or broadcast behind it — a social-media origin, not a documentary one.
